subject: Billing mechanics: context bands, rounding, and pilot floor negotiation
messages:

Subject: Billing mechanics: context bands, rounding, and pilot floor negotiation

Hi Tessa / Vanessa,

Thanks again for the demo yesterday — Velox is excited about Redwood's latency and cost controls. Procurement asked me for a clear, example-driven explanation of how you meter long-context conversations and how the minimums/rounding work in practice. A few specific asks: 

- For a single user session that opens a 12k-token conversation and then generates 3 incremental responses totaling ~2k tokens, how do you bucket the request? Is the entire call billed to a 16k band or is the generated output billed separately?
- What rounding quantum do you apply (do you round every request up to N tokens, and does that quantum change for long-context models)?
- Do you apply a per-session floor (minimum bill) or a per-request minimum? If there is a session floor, how often does it reset?
- For streaming responses, how are tokens attributed and rounded while the stream is open?

If you can attach a sample invoice line showing the math for the scenario above that'd be ideal — Procurement wants a deterministic example they can plug into their TCO model. Also: we'll be running a 3-month pilot. Is there any flexibility to waive the session floor for the pilot or cap it for the initial month?

Happy to jump on a quick call if that's faster.

Best,
Sam

From: tessa_morgan@redwood.com
To: Sam Reynolds <sam.reynolds@veloxsys.com>
Cc: vanessa_ortiz@redwood.com, karthik_iyer@redwood.com
Date: 2026-12-05T11:07:00-08:00
Subject: Re: Billing mechanics: context bands, rounding, and pilot floor negotiation

Sam — thanks for the clear list of asks. Below is a succinct, example-first explanation; attaching a one-line sample invoice (sample-invoice.pdf) and a starter pricing workbook (velox-pilot-pricing.xlsx).

Short summary (TL;DR):
- We tokenize request + response and bill on a per-request basis, using a small billing quantum that increases only for highest-capacity bands.
- Long-contexts are not blindly forced into the largest bucket for the whole session — each API call is metered independently but we expose a session floor policy to protect microcalls.

Example: 12k context, followed by 3 incremental responses (~2k generated total)
1) Initial request: client sends a 12,000-token prompt that stays in the conversation history. Tokenizer reports 12,000 input tokens.
2) Response 1: generation outputs 800 tokens (billing counts both prompt + generated tokens for that call).
3) Response 2: generate 700 tokens.
4) Response 3: generate 500 tokens.

Metering mathematics we apply (conservative but deterministic rules):
- Billing quantum: we bill in 20-token units for standard bands (1 unit = 20 tokens). For higher-capacity 32k+ bands the quantum becomes 80 tokens (to align with backend batching patterns).
- Per-call accounting: each call's billed units = ceil((input_tokens + output_tokens) / quantum).
- Session floor: we apply a per-session floor of 3 units (i.e., 60 tokens equivalent) per 30-minute active window. The floor only applies if the session is active (activity = any API call within the window). If a session is idle for 30+ minutes it resets and the next call is evaluated against a new floor window.
- Streaming: while streaming, tokens are attributed to the open request; we emit interim billing checkpoints every 128 tokens or every 250ms (whichever comes first) and round each checkpoint up to the quantum. That prevents micro-billing on sub-token websocket pings but keeps streaming attribution near-real-time.

Applying that to your scenario:
- Initial call: 12,000 input + 0 output = 12,000 tokens => billed units = ceil(12000 / 20) = 600 units.
- Response 1: input references prompt (we do not double-bill full 12k each time — we bill the actual request size sent; in most SDKs the prompt is a diff or pointer, but for your strict example assume client re-sends 12k each reply): if 12k input + 800 output = 12,800 => ceil(12800 / 20) = 640 units. If SDK uses diffs, typical incremental cost is only for outputs + a small prefix.
- Responses 2 & 3 similar math.
- Session floor: because these calls are in the same active window, the 3-unit floor is effectively irrelevant at these volumes (floor is a protection for tiny, chat-heartbeat style sessions).

Two practical notes:
- For customers using our session token pointers (recommended), we charge full tokenization only when the entire conversation is first ingested; subsequent turns are charged on the incremental prompt + generation delta which dramatically lowers cost for long-lived threads.
- We provide an opt-in "pilot floor waiver" for customers on trial that allows waiving the per-session floor for the first 30 days up to a token cap.

Pilot concession we can offer today:
- Waive the per-session floor for the first 30 days, capped at 50k billed tokens total for the customer across all sessions.
- If Velox commits to a minimum of 500k billed tokens/month for months 2–6, we can apply a 10% usage discount on top of published rates.

I attached the workbook with the two scenarios: (A) naive re-sent-prompt math and (B) session-pointer-optimized math. The sample-invoice.pdf shows line items for 1) billed units, 2) unit price, 3) applied rounding, 4) session-floor credit (if any).

If you want us to waive the 30-day floor without a cap we can do that too, but we prefer the cap for internal cost control during pilots.

Happy to jump on a call to walk through the workbook line-by-line — propose Wed 10:00am PT?

Regards,

Sam — quick follow-up and approval note.

1) Justification for high-band quantum (one-paragraph summary you can drop into procurement packet): 
Redwood increases billing quantum for higher-capacity bands to align metering with backend batching and kernel-selection behavior. Large-context models induce larger memory and IO windows and our serving runtime applies coarser batching to maintain throughput/latency SLAs; the larger quantum reduces per-token metering noise from micro-batches and makes unit economics stable across heavy tails. In short: it is a throughput and determinism tradeoff — the larger quantum matches how we actually consume GPU cycles.

2) Pilot cap: Vanessa and I reviewed with Finance. We can increase the pilot waiver cap to 75,000 billed tokens for the first 30 days. Conditions: 
- Cap applies to billed tokens (post-rounding) across all Velox sessions and projects under the same account ID.
- If you exceed the cap during the 30-day window we'll bill overage at the standard published rate; Finance will notify you when you hit 80% of the cap.
- The 10% committed usage discount still requires a signed commitment for months 2–6 at >= 500k billed tokens/month.

If that matches what you need I'll send a short confirmation email that you can attach to the PO/Legal packet.

Thanks,
Tessa

-----
